case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the maximum civil penalty for a non-willful failure to file a timely and accurate FBAR under the Bank Secrecy Act applies per annual report (per FBAR form) or per unreported foreign account.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 31 U.S.C. §§ 5314 and 5321(a)(5)(A) and (B)(i) (civil penalties for FBAR reporting violations under the Bank Secrecy Act); (Eighth Amendment challenge was raised below but treated as moot in the materials provided).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Bittner argues that for non-willful violations, the statute sets a single maximum penalty tied to the annual FBAR filing obligation (i.e., per report/form per year), not multiplied by the number of accounts. He emphasizes the text and structure of § 5321(a)(5), contends the government’s per-account theory produces disproportionate and 'absurd' outcomes Congress would not have intended for non-willful conduct, and invokes the rule of lenity to resolve any ambiguity in favor of the lower, per-report penalty.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that a non-willful 'violation' occurs with respect to each account that should have been reported, so the $10,000 maximum applies on a per-account basis. The government’s view treats the statutory duty as reporting each foreign account and contends Congress designed the civil penalty scheme to scale with the number of unreported accounts, even for non-willful violations.
key_precedents: Watt v. (citation incomplete in provided excerpt)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that § 5314 is account-directed—reporting a “relation” to a foreign financial agency—so each omitted account might be characterized as a distinct infraction; but that reading lacks a clear statutory hook in the non-willful penalty cap, which speaks in terms of a “violation of[] section 5314” and does not use the account-specific language Congress employed for willful penalties. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Universal C.I.T. Credit Corp. is persuasive under my institutional approach: absent a clear statement, we should not adopt a penalty-multiplying unit that effectively turns on regulatory form design and enforcement discretion. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern reinforces that legitimacy problem—Treasury should not be able to escalate penalties dramatically by structuring the FBAR as many line items rather than a single report. I would keep the holding narrow: for non-willful penalties under § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i), the unit of violation is the failure to file an accurate annual FBAR, while reserving any account-specific questions in the willful context.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest claim—that each unreported account is a separate “violation” because § 5314 is account-focused—still lacks a textual anchor in § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i), which caps “any civil penalty imposed under subparagraph (A)” without adopting account-based language. As Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch stress, Congress expressly made the willful penalty account-calibrated (keyed to “the balance in the account”), and that contrast is powerful evidence that Congress did not silently authorize a per-account multiplier for non-willful penalties. Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability/separation-of-powers concern reinforces the originalist point: allowing Treasury’s form design to define the unit of violation would effectively let the Executive set penalty magnitudes Congress did not clearly enact. Universal C.I.T. Credit Corp., invoked by Barrett, fits our strict-construction approach to punitive civil sanctions by counseling against multiplying penalties absent clear statutory direction, so I remain with the petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that § 5321(a)(5)(A) authorizes penalties for “any violation” of § 5314 and that each undisclosed account could be framed as a separate breach of the account-reporting duty. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 5314 is implemented through regulations requiring a single annual FBAR (one report), and § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) does not supply the account-by-account unit Congress expressly used for willful penalties (e.g., “balance in the account”), making the per-report reading the better textual fit. Barrett’s reliance on Universal C.I.T. Credit Corp. is persuasive here: absent a clear statement, we should resist multiplying penalties by subdividing one reporting obligation into many. The government’s construction would effectively let Treasury’s form design determine penalty magnitude, which—quite apart from any lenity label—counsels against adopting the broader interpretation without clearer statutory direction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The government’s strongest claim—that each unreported account is a separate “violation” of § 5314—still lacks a clear statutory hook in the non-willful cap, which limits “any civil penalty” without adopting the expressly account-calibrated language Congress used for willful penalties keyed to “the balance in the account.” As Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, the legal duty as implemented is to file one annual FBAR, so defining “violation” by line-item/account count effectively lets Treasury’s form design and enforcement choice drive punitive exposure, creating serious fair-notice and disproportionality concerns for concededly non-willful conduct. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Universal C.I.T. Credit Corp. strengthens my view that when Congress has not clearly specified the unit of violation, we should not presume penalty multiplication by implication. On a pragmatic, access-to-justice lens, the per-account approach risks crushing, arbitrary penalties for ordinary taxpayers, and the statute’s structure does not clearly authorize that result.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The government’s strongest point—that §5314 is account-focused and thus each omitted account is a separate “violation”—still runs into the statutory structure and how the duty is operationalized: §5314 authorizes the Secretary to require a single annual “report,” and the regulations implement that as one FBAR, making the non-willful “violation” most naturally the failure to file an accurate report for the year. Justice Barrett’s structural contrast is the key textual answer: Congress expressly made willful penalties account-calibrated (“balance in the account”) in §5321(a)(5)(D), but did not use account-specific language in the non-willful cap, which is strong evidence against importing a per-account multiplier by implication. Universal C.I.T., as Barrett and the Chief emphasize, reinforces our reluctance to multiply penalties without a clear congressional unit of offense—especially where, as Justice Gorsuch notes, the per-account view effectively lets form design and enforcement discretion determine penalty magnitude. Nothing in the opposing argument overcomes those textual and administrability concerns, so I remain with Petitioner.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that § 5314 is account-centered (“a relation … with a foreign financial agency”), so each omitted account could be cast as its own violation; but § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) caps “any civil penalty imposed under subparagraph (A)” for a “violation” of § 5314, whose operative command is to file a “report” as prescribed—implemented here as one annual FBAR. As Justice Barrett stresses via Universal C.I.T. Credit Corp., absent a clear statement we should not multiply penalties by subdividing a single reporting duty into multiple infractions, especially where Congress elsewhere in the same subsection used unmistakably account-calibrated language for willful penalties (“balance in the account”). Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional concern reinforces the textual point: a per-account rule effectively lets regulatory form design and line-item counting determine statutory penalty magnitude, raising separation-of-powers and fair-notice problems in a punitive civil regime. Nothing in Shultz (as Justice Thomas notes) undermines this; if anything, it confirms penalties attach to the reporting obligation the regulations define, which is annual and report-based.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point remains that § 5314 is account-focused and thus each omitted account could be a distinct “violation,” but that reading does not square with how Congress drafted the non-willful cap in § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i): it limits the penalty for “any violation” without the account-calibrating language Congress explicitly used for willful penalties keyed to “the balance in the account.” Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability/legitimacy concern and Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers point sharpen why we should hesitate to let penalty magnitude hinge on Treasury’s form design and line-item counting absent a clear statement from Congress. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Universal C.I.T. Credit Corp. fits our traditional approach to penalty provisions: when the unit of violation is at least ambiguous, we do not presume Congress silently authorized penalty multiplication. On this text-and-structure reading, the most natural unit for non-willful penalties is the annual FBAR/reporting failure, so I remain with Petitioner.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The government’s strongest contention—that § 5314 is account-focused so each omitted account is a separate “violation”—still lacks a firm textual foothold in § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i), which caps the penalty for a non-willful “violation of[] section 5314” without using account-calibrating terms Congress employed elsewhere (notably the willful “balance in the account” language). Chief Justice Roberts’s point that § 5314’s operative duty is defined through regulations requiring a single annual FBAR report remains decisive for me: the most natural unit of non-willful “violation” is the failure to file an accurate report for the year, not each line item within it. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern reinforces the textual one: a per-account multiplier effectively lets Treasury’s form design determine penalty magnitude absent clear congressional authorization. Universal C.I.T.’s caution against penalty multiplication in the face of statutory uncertainty continues to support the per-report construction rather than expanding liability by implication.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Government’s strongest argument—that § 5314 is account-focused so each omitted account is a separate “violation”—still founders on the statutory design: § 5314 creates a reporting duty “in the manner” the Secretary prescribes, and Treasury has implemented that duty as a single annual FBAR, making the administrable and fair unit the report-year. Justice Kagan’s structural point remains most persuasive to me: Congress expressly made willful penalties account-calibrated by referencing “the balance in the account,” yet did not use similar account-specific language for non-willful penalties, which counsels against importing an account multiplier by implication. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Universal C.I.T. reinforces my view that we should not multiply punitive civil penalties absent a clear congressional statement—especially where a per-account rule would let regulatory form design and enforcement choice drive enormous, disproportionate liability for concededly non-willful conduct. Nothing in colleagues’ discussion undermines the fair-notice and practical-consequences concerns Justice Sotomayor highlighted, so I remain with Petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 5321(a)(5)(A) authorizes a penalty for any “violation” of § 5314, and for non-willful conduct § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) sets a $10,000 maximum without tying that cap to each “account,” a term Congress used elsewhere in the same penalty subsection when it wished to do so. Reading “violation” to mean the annual failure to file an accurate FBAR (the report required by § 5314’s implementing regulations) yields a narrower, more administrable rule that avoids large, account-multiplying penalties for concededly non-willful conduct—an outcome that risks undermining institutional legitimacy and invites excessive-fines concerns. Boyd supports construing the non-willful cap on a per-report basis, and absent clearer statutory direction, any remaining ambiguity counsels against the government’s expansive per-account aggregation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text Congress enacted in 31 U.S.C. § 5321(a)(5)(A) authorizes a penalty for a person who “violates … any provision of section 5314,” and § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) then caps “the amount of any civil penalty imposed under subparagraph (A)” at $10,000—indicating a single penalty per “violation” of the reporting obligation created by § 5314 and its implementing regulations. Section 5314 directs the Secretary to require reports “in the way and to the extent the Secretary prescribes,” and the implementing regime requires an annual FBAR filing (31 C.F.R. § 1010.306), so the most natural original public meaning of “violation” for non-willful conduct is the failure to file a timely and accurate annual report, not each account entry within that report. Reading “violation” to mean per account would effectively rewrite the statutory cap by multiplying $10,000 across accounts, a result not grounded in the statute’s text or the regulatory structure that defines the duty. Consistent with Shultz v. United States, 416 U.S. 21 (1974), penalties attach upon violation of the Secretary’s reporting regulations, which here point to the annual filing obligation as the unit of violation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 31 U.S.C. § 5321(a)(5)(A) authorizes a penalty for “any violation” of § 5314, and the implementing scheme contemplates a single annual FBAR filing obligation—one report that may list multiple accounts—so the most natural unit of “violation” for non-willful conduct is the failure to file an accurate and timely report for that year. Reading “violation” to mean each unreported account would transform a single filing lapse into dozens of separate penalties without clear statutory direction, producing outsized consequences for concededly non-willful conduct and undermining the statute’s instruction to avoid “unreasonabl[e]” reporting burdens. Where Congress wanted account-sensitive scaling, it spoke more clearly in the willful provisions of § 5321(a)(5)(C)–(D), and ambiguity in a punitive monetary-penalty statute should be strictly construed against the Government. The Ninth Circuit’s per-form approach in United States v. Boyd reflects that ordinary understanding of the annual FBAR duty and avoids importing a per-item multiplier that the non-willful text does not clearly command.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 5321(a)(5)(A) caps the non-willful penalty at $10,000 per “violation,” and in this context the operative violation is the failure to file a timely and accurate annual FBAR required by § 5314, not a separate infraction for each account listed on that form. Reading “violation” to mean per-account for non-willful conduct risks crushing, disproportionate penalties untethered to culpability and inconsistent with fair-notice principles that apply to punitive monetary sanctions, see FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 567 U.S. 239, 253 (2012). Any genuine ambiguity in the unit of violation should be resolved against multiplying penalties, consistent with the traditional strict construction of penal laws and the separation-of-powers and notice concerns reflected in United States v. Wiltberger, 18 U.S. (5 Wheat.) 76, 95 (1820). The government’s per-account approach may be appropriate for willful violations where Congress clearly escalated sanctions, § 5321(a)(5)(C)-(D), but it is not clearly stated for non-willful violations and should not be presumed.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 5321(a)(5)(A) authorizes a penalty for “any violation” of §5314, and §5314’s obligation is to file an annual report in the manner the Secretary prescribes—one FBAR form that aggregates all reportable accounts—so the most coherent reading is that a non-willful “violation” is a failure to file a timely and accurate annual report, not a separate violation for each line item on that report. The government’s per-account construction sits awkwardly with §5321(a)(5)(B)(i), which expressly keys willful penalties to “the balance in the account,” suggesting Congress knew how to make penalties account-specific when it wanted to, and it risks unworkable, highly disproportionate outcomes for concededly non-willful conduct. Where the text and structure at least leave genuine ambiguity about the unit of violation in a civil-penalty regime with punitive effect, that doubt should be resolved against multiplying penalties absent clear congressional direction. Boyd underscores that the dispute turns on defining the “violation,” and the better statutory fit is per-FBAR-per-year.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 5321(a)(5)(A) authorizes a penalty for violating “any provision of section 5314,” and § 5314’s text speaks in terms of filing an annual “report” containing information “in the way and to the extent the Secretary prescribes,” which most naturally ties the non-willful penalty cap in § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) to the failure to file an accurate, timely FBAR (a per-report duty), not to each account listed on the form. Congress showed it knew how to calibrate penalties on an account-by-account basis when it wished—e.g., the willful penalty references “the balance in the account at the time of the violation,” § 5321(a)(5)(D)(ii)—but it did not use similarly account-specific language for non-willful violations. Reading “violation” to mean each unreported account would allow massive multiplication untethered to the statutory maximum Congress set, and any residual ambiguity in a punitive civil penalty provision should be resolved in favor of the citizen under the rule of lenity. The government’s approach also risks effectively delegating the size of penalties to form design and regulatory detail, raising separation-of-powers concerns inconsistent with a strict textual reading of §§ 5314 and 5321(a)(5).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 5321(a)(5)(A) authorizes a penalty for a “violation of” § 5314, and the most natural reading—consistent with the reporting regime—treats the relevant violation for non-willful cases as the failure to file a timely and accurate annual FBAR, not a separate violation for each account listed (or omitted) within that single required report. The statutory structure reinforces that view: Congress expressly keyed willful penalties to “the balance in the account,” § 5321(a)(5)(D), suggesting that when it wanted an account-by-account metric it said so, whereas the non-willful cap in § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) speaks in report-based terms (“any violation”) without an account-based measure. A per-account maximum for non-willful conduct risks severe, hard-to-administer, and potentially arbitrary outcomes that Congress likely reserved for willful violations, and it would create substantial variability and enforcement discretion inconsistent with practical workability and institutional stability. To the extent “violation” is genuinely ambiguous in this civil-penalty setting, the rule-of-lenity-style canon for punitive monetary sanctions supports adopting the narrower, per-report construction, and the Ninth Circuit’s contrary approach in United States v. Boyd is unpersuasive.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 5321(a)(5)(A) authorizes a penalty for a “violation of[] section 5314,” and § 5314—read with the implementing regulations—imposes an annual obligation to file a single report (an FBAR) disclosing specified foreign-account information, not a freestanding, separately penalized duty for each account. The statutory text for the non-willful penalty notably does not speak in per-account terms (unlike other provisions that do), and the structure of § 5321(a)(5) distinguishes willful violations (where Congress expressly calibrated penalties to the “balance in the account”) from non-willful ones, signaling a different unit for non-willful penalties. Where Congress has not clearly specified the unit of violation, the Court has cautioned against multiplying penalties absent clear textual direction, see United States v. Universal C.I.T. Credit Corp., 344 U.S. 218, 224–26 (1952), and the Ninth Circuit’s per-form reading in United States v. Boyd is consistent with that approach. At minimum, any lingering ambiguity about the unit of violation after exhausting ordinary tools of interpretation should be resolved against the government’s penalty-multiplying construction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 5321(a)(5)(A) authorizes a penalty for “any violation” of § 5314, and for non-willful conduct § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) sets a $10,000 maximum without clearly specifying that the unit of violation is each individual account rather than the annual reporting obligation implemented through the FBAR. Given that ambiguity, principles of procedural fairness and the practical consequences of multiplying penalties based on account count—potentially producing crushing liability for the least culpable, non-willful filers—counsel a per-report (per year) construction. That approach also aligns with the rule that one should not be subjected to a civil penalty unless the statute plainly imposes it, as recognized in Commissioner v. Acker, 361 U.S. 87, 91 (1959). Where Congress intended account-specific scaling, it said so expressly elsewhere in § 5321(a)(5), reinforcing that the non-willful maximum should not be expanded by implication.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Bank Secrecy Act’s $10,000 maximum penalty for a non-willful FBAR violation applies per annual FBAR form filed late/incorrectly, or instead applies per foreign account that was not properly reported on the FBAR.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 31 U.S.C. § 5321(a)(5)(A) and § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) (civil penalties for non-willful violations of FBAR reporting requirements under 31 U.S.C. § 5314); petitioner also raised an Eighth Amendment excessive-fines issue below (treated as moot in the district court).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Bittner argues that for non-willful conduct the statute ties the penalty to a reporting violation (i.e., the failure to timely/file an accurate FBAR form), so the maximum $10,000 penalty should be assessed per FBAR filing obligation per year—not multiplied by the number of accounts—both because the statutory text targets the reporting requirement and because a per-account reading would create disproportionately large, arguably absurd penalties for non-willful errors; to the extent there is ambiguity, he invokes lenity-like principles and related canons favoring the narrower penalty construction.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that the relevant 'violation' is the failure to report each required foreign account, so a non-willful penalty may be assessed up to $10,000 for each unreported account per year; the government emphasizes that § 5314 requires reporting of 'a relation' with a 'foreign financial agency' and implementing rules are account-focused, so treating each account as a separate reporting duty best fits the statutory scheme and enforcement purpose, and the rule of lenity should not narrow a civil penalty regime in the way petitioner suggests.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that § 5314’s account-focused implementation means each omitted account is a separate “violation”—has intuitive force, but it still asks us to let regulatory detail supply the statutory unit of maximum liability where Congress did not speak clearly in § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i). As Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress in the same subsection used unmistakably account/balance-based language for willful violations, which makes it difficult to infer that the non-willful cap silently turns on each account rather than the annual reporting obligation. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern is also persuasive under my institutional-legitimacy lens: we should avoid a construction that effectively allows form design to ratchet up statutory maxima absent a clear statement from Congress. Acker’s strict-construction principle for penalty provisions, cited by Justice Kagan, supports resolving any residual ambiguity in favor of the narrower per-report cap, allowing us to decide on narrow statutory grounds and sidestep unnecessary constitutional issues.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that § 5314’s implementing regulations require account-specific disclosures, so omitting multiple accounts is multiple “violations.” But under a strict textualist/originalist approach, the penalty unit must come from Congress’s text: § 5314 imposes a duty to file a “report” in the manner the Secretary prescribes, and § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) caps “any such violation” without the account-specific language Congress expressly used for willful penalties (as Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice emphasize). Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern is decisive for me: allowing regulatory “way and extent” details to multiply the statutory maximum would let the Executive expand punishment through form design rather than clear legislative command. Commissioner v. Acker, invoked by Justice Kagan, reinforces that any residual ambiguity in a punitive civil-penalty provision should be resolved against the harsher construction, so I remain with petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest pushback is Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers point—concern that agency form design could effectively ratchet up maximum liability—but that objection overstates what is happening here because § 5314 itself delegates the “way and … extent” of the required report, and Treasury’s account-by-account specification is an implementation of the statutory duty, not an executive invention of a new penalty unit. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress that Congress used explicit account/balance language for willful penalties, but that negative-implication argument is not strong enough to overcome § 5314’s account-centered disclosure regime; Congress can sensibly measure willful and non-willful penalties differently without collapsing the underlying unit of noncompliance. Acker’s strict-construction principle, invoked by Justice Kagan, matters only if the statute is genuinely in equipoise; here the text/structure point toward multiple “violations” when multiple required account disclosures are omitted. Finally, the per-report reading invites a substantial under-deterrence loophole for multi-account nonreporting that is hard to reconcile with Congress’s evident aim to secure comprehensive foreign-account transparency.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that § 5314’s delegated “way and extent” authority makes the disclosure regime functionally account-specific—still does not answer the antecedent question of what Congress made the unit of “any such violation” for a punitive cap in § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i). As Justice Gorsuch and the Chief Justice stress, accepting the government’s per-account theory effectively lets Treasury’s form design and regulatory granularity ratchet up the statutory maximum without a clear congressional statement, aggravating fair-notice concerns in a non-willful penalty regime. Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan’s structural point reinforces that Congress knew how to legislate in expressly account- and balance-based terms in the willful provisions, and its choice not to do so here is telling. Deterrence concerns are real, but for non-willful mistakes I cannot read ambiguity to authorize potentially ruinous multipliers absent unmistakable text, especially where a per-report reading avoids needless due process and Excessive Fines friction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s deterrence point is the best case for the government, but it cannot supply the unit of “violation” where Congress did not clearly choose a per-account multiplier; § 5314 imposes an obligation to file a “report” in the way and to the extent the Secretary prescribes, and § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) caps “any such violation” at $10,000 without the account/balance language Congress used in the adjacent willful provisions (as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize). I agree with Justice Gorsuch that reading the cap to turn on regulatory line-item design risks letting the Executive effectively expand maximum penalties through form architecture rather than enacted text, which undermines statutory coherence and separation of powers. Commissioner v. Acker, raised in our discussion, strengthens the strict-construction instinct in punitive civil-penalty statutes: when “violation” plausibly means the annual FBAR/reporting failure, we should not infer the harsher per-account regime absent clear words. Alito’s account-focused “extent” argument shows how Treasury can collect account-by-account information, but it doesn’t convincingly transform the statutory cap into a per-account penalty unit.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that § 5314’s implementing regulations demand account-by-account detail, so each omitted account is a separate breach, and he frames the regulation as merely specifying the delegated “way and extent” of the report. But even accepting the delegation, § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) is the penalty-setting provision, and it caps “any such violation” at $10,000 without adopting the account-based unit Congress used elsewhere—most notably, as Justice Barrett stresses, the willful-penalty language keyed expressly to “the balance in the account.” Under a separation-of-powers and strict-construction approach to punitive civil penalties (as Justice Kagan notes via Acker), we should not let regulatory form design supply the multiplier that increases maximum liability absent a clear congressional statement. Alito’s under-deterrence concern is a policy argument for Congress, not a basis for reading “violation” to mean each line item when the statute can naturally be read to treat the annual FBAR filing obligation as the unit.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that § 5314’s regime, as implemented, requires account-by-account disclosures, so each omitted account can be characterized as a separate breach. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch stress, the penalty statute keys liability to a “violation of” § 5314, and § 5314 speaks in terms of filing “reports” in the manner the Secretary prescribes—so regulations and form design can specify the content of the report, but should not silently supply the unit that multiplies the statutory maximum. Justice Barrett’s structural point is decisive for me: Congress used unmistakably account/balance-based language for willful penalties, and its absence in the non-willful cap makes it hard to infer a per-account multiplier without clearer text. Given the punitive practical consequences, Acker’s strict-construction principle reinforces that any residual ambiguity should be resolved against the harsher, per-account reading.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that § 5314’s delegation to prescribe the report’s “way and extent” makes the disclosure obligation effectively account-by-account, so each omitted account is a separate breach. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, the penalty authority in § 5321(a)(5)(A)–(B)(i) is keyed to a “violation of” § 5314 and caps “any such violation” at $10,000 without adopting an account-based unit; reading regulations to supply that unit would let executive form design expand the statutory maximum, an outcome I find hard to square with textualism in a punitive civil-penalty provision. The structural contrast Justice Kagan highlights—Congress’s explicit account/balance-based language for willful penalties—strengthens the negative implication that Congress did not silently choose a per-account multiplier for non-willful violations. And to the extent ambiguity remains, Acker’s strict-construction principle for penalty statutes supports the per-report cap, so I do not see Alito’s deterrence rationale as sufficient to overcome the statutory text and structure.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that § 5314’s delegated “way and extent” language, as operationalized by Treasury’s account-specific regulations, makes each omitted account a separate violation—has real force as a compliance and deterrence matter. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, that move effectively allows regulatory form design to set the penalty unit and thereby expand maximum liability without a clear congressional statement in § 5321(a)(5)(B)(i), which is especially troubling in a punitive civil-penalty regime implicating fair-notice principles. Justice Barrett’s structural point reinforces this: Congress used unmistakably account/balance-based language for willful penalties, so the absence of comparable per-account language for non-willful violations is best read to cap the annual reporting failure rather than multiply by line items. Acker-style strict construction, invoked by Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh, doesn’t decide the case alone, but it confirms my pragmatic concern that ambiguity should not be resolved to impose unexpectedly severe aggregate penalties on concededly non-willful actors.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 5321(a)(5)(A) authorizes a penalty for “any violation” of § 5314’s reporting requirement, and § 5314 directs that reports “shall contain” information “in the way and to the extent the Secretary prescribes,” suggesting the relevant duty is the annual report (FBAR) rather than each line item within it. Reading “violation” to mean each unreported account would turn a single filing obligation into potentially massive aggregate penalties for non-willful errors, raising serious proportionality concerns and inviting unnecessary constitutional disputes (including the Excessive Fines issue raised below) that we should avoid if the statute can be read more narrowly. Where the statute does not clearly specify a per-account unit, the better course—consistent with our institutional role and narrow decisionmaking—is to adopt the construction that attaches the $10,000 cap to the non-willful failure to file an accurate and timely FBAR for a given year. This approach respects federalism and enforcement discretion while adhering to the text Congress enacted and avoiding an expansive penalty interpretation absent clear authorization.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The statutory text makes the non-willful penalty turn on a “violation” of the reporting requirement imposed under § 5314, and that requirement is implemented as a single annual FBAR filing obligation rather than an account-by-account filing obligation. When Congress intended to speak in account-focused terms, it did so expressly—e.g., in § 5321(a)(5)(B)(ii)’s reasonable-cause provision referring to “the balance in the account”—confirming by negative implication that § 5321(a)(5)(A)–(B)(i) does not impose per-account penalties. A per-form reading better accords with the original public meaning of “violation” as the breach of the legally required act (filing the report) and avoids expanding federal penalties beyond what the text clearly authorizes, consistent with principles of narrow construction in penalty provisions. Where the government seeks a harsher construction untethered to the enacted words, we should adhere to the statute’s text and structure rather than policy-driven enforcement aims.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 5321(a)(5)(A) authorizes a penalty for a “violation of[] any provision of section 5314,” and § 5314’s reporting duty—implemented through Treasury’s account-specific regulations—centers on identifying each reportable foreign account relationship, making each omitted account a separate “violation” under the statute. Reading “violation” per account better fits the structure of the BSA’s enforcement scheme and avoids creating an easy loophole whereby a filer with dozens of accounts would face the same maximum penalty as a filer with one, undermining deterrence and compliance. The Court’s civil-penalty cases caution against expansive penalties not clearly authorized, but they also turn on the statutory unit of wrongdoing; here the unit of required disclosure is the account, not the form. Any lenity-like strict construction principles drawn from revenue-penalty decisions (e.g., Commissioner v. Acker) do not justify collapsing multiple distinct reporting omissions into a single annual cap where the statutory and regulatory scheme is account-focused.
